chapter_title: Environmental Sensors: Temperature, Humidity, Light, and Motion
chapter_summary:
Sensors are the input devices that let a Raspberry Pi perceive the physical world. Environmental sensors measure conditions such as temperature, humidity, light, and motion. Each sensor produces an electrical signal that the Pi can read and convert into useful information.

The DHT11 and DHT22 are popular digital temperature and humidity sensors. The DHT11 is cheaper and less accurate, with a temperature accuracy of about ±2°C and humidity accuracy of about ±5%. The DHT22 is more accurate and has a wider range, but it is slightly more expensive. Both sensors use a single-wire protocol that requires precise timing, so they cannot be read with a simple `Button` class. Instead, you use the `Adafruit_DHT` library or `dht11` package.

To read a DHT22 connected to GPIO 4:

```python
import Adafruit_DHT

sensor = Adafruit_DHT.DHT22
pin = 4

humidity, temperature = Adafruit_DHT.read_retry(sensor, pin)

if humidity is not None and temperature is not None:
    print(f"Temp: {temperature:.1f}°C, Humidity: {humidity:.1f}%")
else:
    print("Failed to read sensor")
```

A more modern approach uses the `gpiozero` `DHT22` device or the `adafruit-circuitpython-dht` library. The `adafruit-circuitpython-dht` library requires the `libgpiod2` system package and works well on Raspberry Pi OS Bookworm.

A light-dependent resistor, or LDR, changes resistance based on light intensity. Because the Raspberry Pi has no analog inputs, you use an MCP3008 ADC, as described in the previous module. Connect the LDR in a voltage divider with a fixed resistor, usually 10kΩ, between 3.3V and ground. The junction between the LDR and the resistor connects to an ADC channel. In bright light, the LDR resistance is low, so the ADC reads a high voltage. In darkness, the LDR resistance is high, so the ADC reads a low voltage.

PIR, or Passive Infrared, sensors detect motion by sensing changes in infrared radiation. Warm bodies such as humans emit infrared light. A PIR sensor outputs a HIGH signal when it detects motion. On the Raspberry Pi, a PIR sensor can be connected directly to a GPIO pin because it usually operates at 3.3V or has a 3.3V-compatible output. Use the `gpiozero` `MotionSensor` class:

```python
from gpiozero import MotionSensor
from time import sleep

pir = MotionSensor(18)

while True:
    if pir.motion_detected:
        print("Motion detected!")
    else:
        print("No motion")
    sleep(1)
```

PIR sensors usually have two potentiometers for adjusting sensitivity and the time the output stays HIGH after detection. Event-based code is often better than polling:

```python
from gpiozero import MotionSensor, LED

pir = MotionSensor(18)
led = LED(17)

pir.when_motion = led.on
pir.when_no_motion = led.off

input("Press Enter to exit...")
```

Calibration and error handling are essential with sensors. DHT sensors sometimes return `None` due to timing issues. Always check for valid readings before using them. LDR readings depend on the specific resistor and lighting conditions, so record minimum and maximum values under known conditions and map the output to a percentage.

narration.text: In this chapter you will learn how a Raspberry Pi reads four common environmental sensors and why each one needs a slightly different approach. We will cover digital temperature and humidity sensors that speak a timed single-wire protocol, how to measure ambient light with a resistor and an analog to digital converter, and how passive infrared motion sensors report presence. You will see practical wiring patterns, example code you can run in a terminal, and troubleshooting steps for common failures such as timeouts and invalid readings. This matters because sensors are not perfect: their electrical behavior, timing needs, and required supporting hardware determine which libraries and wiring patterns you use. For example, some sensors emit a clean digital HIGH or LOW while others produce an analog voltage that must be measured with an ADC. By the end of the chapter you will be able to connect a DHT22 to a GPIO pin, read an LDR through an MCP3008, and respond to a PIR event, with basic calibration and error handling in place. Think of this chapter as the toolkit that turns raw signals into reliable inputs for projects, and as you progress consider what assumptions each sensor makes about timing, voltage, and environmental range.

screens.title: Sensors and Signals: Digital vs Analog
screens.subtitle: Why the Raspberry Pi needs different hardware for different sensors

narration.text: Sensors convert physical phenomena into electrical signals. On a Raspberry Pi some sensors provide digital outputs and others produce analog voltages. A digital sensor, such as a PIR or a DHT device, gives clear logical states or a timed digital sequence that a library can decode. A PIR outputs a HIGH when it detects motion, and a DHT uses a single-wire protocol that requires precise timing to parse temperature and humidity. An analog sensor like an LDR varies its resistance with light, producing a continuous voltage in a voltage divider. The Pi has no native analog inputs, so an ADC such as the MCP3008 is required to convert that voltage into a numeric value. A common misconception is to assume that any sensor can be read directly from a GPIO; instead check whether the output is digital or analog and whether the device needs special timing or a library. For example, a DHT22 must be read with a DHT-aware library because its timing-sensitive single-wire protocol cannot be reliably sampled with a generic input read. The takeaway is to always match the sensor's electrical output to the Pi's input method and supporting hardware.

keyIdea.title: Match signal to hardware
keyIdea.text: Digital signals can go to GPIO; analog signals need an ADC. Timing-sensitive sensors require dedicated libraries.

Common misconception

Why it matters: picking the wrong input method can produce sporadic data, false triggers, or hardware damage. When in doubt, consult the sensor's output type and plan for retries and calibration.

screens.title: DHT11 and DHT22: Temperature and Humidity Sensors
screens.subtitle: Compare capabilities and why you might choose one over the other

narration.text: DHT11 and DHT22 are widely used digital sensors for temperature and humidity. The DHT11 is inexpensive but less accurate, with roughly plus or minus two degrees Celsius for temperature and about plus or minus five percent for humidity. The DHT22 is more accurate and supports a wider environmental range at slightly higher cost. Both use a single-wire, timing-sensitive protocol that sends a sequence of pulses the host must decode. Because of that timing, you should use a dedicated library rather than attempting to bit-bang the protocol with naive waits. A typical way to read a DHT22 in Python is to use the Adafruit DHT library or modern alternatives such as gpiozero's DHT device or the adafruit circuitpython dht package. When a read fails the library may return None values, so your code must check for valid values before printing or storing them. One common pitfall is to assume every read will succeed; adding a retry or a fallback value prevents crashes and improves reliability in real-world deployments. screens.title: LDRs and Voltage Dividers
screens.subtitle: Turning light-dependent resistance into a measurable voltage

narration.text: An LDR, or light-dependent resistor, changes its resistance based on how much light falls on its surface. To read that change with a Raspberry Pi you form a voltage divider: the LDR and a fixed resistor, commonly ten kilo ohms, are connected between 3.3 volts and ground. The controller reads the voltage at the junction between the LDR and the fixed resistor. In bright light the LDR resistance is low and the junction voltage is closer to three point three volts, so the ADC reports a high value. In darkness the LDR resistance is high and the junction voltage falls toward ground, producing a low ADC reading. Because the Pi lacks native analog inputs you use an MCP3008 ADC and feed the junction to one channel. A practical calibration step is to record the ADC reading in known dark and bright conditions, then map the raw value linearly to a percentage. A common error is choosing the wrong fixed resistor value; ten kilo ohms is a good starting point but you may change it to suit your LDR and the light range you expect.

keyIdea.title: Voltage divider rule
keyIdea.text: Use an LDR with a 10k resistor between 3.3V and ground; read the junction with an ADC and map raw counts to a percentage.

Module 5 › Chapter 5.1 › LDR & ADC
Definition

LDR with voltage divider

Create a divider using the LDR and a fixed 10k resistor, then read the junction with an MCP3008 channel to obtain a usable numeric value.

Why the ADC is needed

The Pi's GPIO pins are digital only. The MCP3008 converts analog voltage into a digital count the Pi can read over SPI.

Key Takeaway

Record dark and bright ADC baselines, then map raw counts into a percentage for consistent readings across setups.

Concrete Example
ADC raw values: 20 in darkness, 1020 in bright light. Mapped percent = (raw - min) / (max - min) * 100
Common misconception

Assuming raw ADC values are directly comparable across different LDRs or resistor choices. Always calibrate your specific circuit and environment.

Practical tip: start with a 10k fixed resistor and test bright and dark baselines before deciding to change resistance for a different reading range.

narration.text: To read an LDR with the Raspberry Pi you will follow a short process that starts with wiring and ends with mapping raw ADC values to a percentage. First, wire a voltage divider between 3.3 volts and ground using the LDR and a 10 kilo ohm fixed resistor. Connect the junction to an MCP3008 channel and ensure the MCP3008 shares SPI pins and ground with the Pi. Second, enable SPI and install a Python SPI or MCP3008 helper library. Third, read raw ADC counts and record values under known conditions: take a reading in darkness and one in bright light to get minimum and maximum baselines. Fourth, map raw counts to a percentage using a linear mapping and clamp values to zero to one hundred percent. A common mistake is reading a single baseline and assuming it applies across environments; instead record ranges where your project will operate. This step-based pattern helps you get repeatable, interpretable light measurements ready for logging or control decisions. screens.title: PIR Motion Sensors
screens.subtitle: How passive infrared sensing detects movement and how to wire it

narration.text: PIR stands for Passive Infrared. These sensors monitor changes in infrared radiation in front of them, which allows them to detect warm moving bodies like humans. When a change is detected the sensor typically outputs a digital HIGH. Most PIR modules are 3.3 volt compatible or have a 3.3 volt tolerant output, so they can be connected directly to a Raspberry Pi GPIO pin and read in software. A typical physical module includes two potentiometers: one to adjust sensitivity and one to set the time the output stays HIGH after detection. Wiring is straightforward: connect power, ground, and the data pin to a GPIO, and ensure a common ground between the Pi and the sensor. A common pitfall is constant triggering due to reflections or improper sensitivity settings; adjust the sensor's potentiometers and test in the real environment. Prefer event-driven code so your program reacts immediately without continuously polling the input pin. screens.title: PIR Polling vs Event-driven Code
screens.subtitle: Why event callbacks are preferred and how to wire a response

narration.text: There are two common ways to read a PIR sensor: polling the GPIO in a loop or using event-driven callbacks. Polling checks the input repeatedly and may print motion or no motion at intervals. While simple, polling wastes C P U and can miss short changes between polls. Event-driven code uses the gpiozero MotionSensor class to attach handlers that run when motion starts and when it stops. This is more efficient and responsive. A common example is to wire the PIR data pin to GPIO eighteen and an LED to GPIO seventeen; then set when motion to turn the LED on and when no motion to turn it off. This event pattern avoids busy loops and keeps your terminal output meaningful because you only see messages when state changes. A misconception is believing polling is more reliable; in practice event callbacks provide immediate responses and are easier to combine with other tasks without blocking the main loop. Comparison

Polling vs Events

Polling loops repeatedly inspect motion state and often sleep between checks. Event-driven code registers functions that run when motion starts or stops, leaving the system idle until a real input arrives.
Why events win

They provide immediate response, lower CPU usage, and cleaner integration with other non-blocking code.

Concrete Example
Terminal output using events: Motion detected! LED on No motion LED off
Practical tip: use events when you need responsiveness or when the Pi must do other tasks. Reserve polling for quick diagnostic checks in the terminal during wiring or initial testing.

screens.title: Calibration and Error Handling
screens.subtitle: Practical steps to make sensor readings reliable

narration.text: Calibration and error handling are essential to make sensor data trustworthy. For DHT sensors, implement a simple retry pattern and check returned values for None before using them. Log failed reads and apply a short delay before retrying to avoid hammering the sensor. For LDRs, record minimum and maximum ADC baselines under known conditions so you can map raw counts into a consistent percentage. Save these baseline values to a small configuration or a local file so they persist across reboots. For PIR sensors, fine tune the sensitivity and the hold time with the onboard potentiometers, and test in the actual installation environment to reduce false positives. A common mistake is to accept the first measured baseline as universal. Instead capture multiple baseline readings over time and under different lighting situations. Error handling ensures that transient failures do not cascade into bad control decisions or data corruption, while calibration makes readings comparable and actionable. screens.title: Troubleshooting Common Failures
screens.subtitle: Checks and fixes for DHT read failures, ADC anomalies, and PIR false triggers

narration.text: When sensors misbehave, a small checklist helps isolate hardware, wiring, or software issues. For DHT failures check the data pin connection and ensure the sensor is powered at three point three volts, not five volts, and that the data pin is not shared with other devices. If reads return None, add retries and a delay between attempts, and verify you are using a timing-aware library. For ADC anomalies like full-scale or zero readings, confirm the MCP3008 has correct power and ground, SPI is enabled, and the channel connected matches your wiring. For LDR values stuck at extremes inspect the voltage divider wiring and try a different fixed resistor value. For PIR false triggers adjust the sensitivity potentiometer and test at the detector's installation height and environment to avoid reflections. Logging timestamps and raw values helps you correlate failures to events such as C P U load or environmental changes. A disciplined approach to log, isolate, adjust, and retest will quickly resolve most common sensor issues. screens.title: Key Concepts — What to Remember
screens.subtitle: Three compact reminders to carry into your projects

narration.text: First, always identify whether a sensor is digital, analog, or timing-sensitive and match it to the correct Raspberry Pi input method. Digital sensors like PIR can go to GPIO; analog sensors require an ADC such as the MCP3008; timing-sensitive sensors like DHT22 need a dedicated library. Second, calibration and validation make readings actionable. Record LDR baselines and map raw ADC counts to percentages, and gate database writes on successful DHT reads to avoid storing invalid values. Third, prefer event-driven code for motion sensing to reduce C P U load and improve responsiveness. Tune PIR sensitivity and hold time on the module for your environment. These three ideas will keep your sensor projects robust and easier to debug. As you build, log well, test in place, and add simple retry and fallback logic to handle noisy real-world signals.
